title: ⭐ Practice: the words and the forms of giving

questions.prompt: After the floods, a company sends the victims blankets, medicine and two lorries instead of a cheque. What has it given?
questions.explanation: Goods, commodities or services given instead of money are "in-kind contributions", and blankets, medicine and lorries are exactly that. "an endowment" is a permanent fund whose income pays for something year after year, and nothing here is invested. "a bequest" is what somebody leaves in a will, while this company is alive and giving now. "a fund-raising campaign" collects money from other people, whereas this company hands over its own goods directly.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The blood bank ___ more than two hundred donors last April."
questions.explanation: last April names a month that is over, and a named finished time takes the simple past, so the bank "welcomed" its donors. "has welcomed" is a present perfect, and the present perfect always refuses a finished time-period such as last April. "has been welcoming" refuses it for the same reason and insists on an activity that has not stopped. "is welcoming" puts the whole of last April into a present continuous, which describes what is going on at the moment of speaking.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The association organises a ___ dinner every spring to pay for the school bags."
questions.explanation: A compound adjective in front of a noun is built on the pattern noun plus -ing, so the dinner is a "fund-raising" dinner: it raises funds. "funds-raising" puts a plural -s inside the compound, and the first word of a compound adjective never takes one. "fund-raise" is the bare verb and cannot describe a noun. "fund-raised" is a past participle and would say that somebody had raised the dinner itself.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The shelter is full. It ___ two more rooms before the winter."
questions.explanation: need is an ordinary full verb: it takes a noun object directly, and the subject It is singular in the present, so the form is "needs" two more rooms. "need" drops the -s that a singular subject requires in the present. "needs to" adds the to that need takes only before another verb, as in needs to open, never before a noun. "is needing" puts a verb of state into the continuous, which English does not do with need.

questions.prompt: Somebody has just claimed that this street gave nothing during the floods. Complete the reply with the emphatic form, so that it insists the fact is true: "The shops of this street ___ four hundred meals a week."
questions.explanation: The emphatic form of a simple past is did plus the base verb, which is how you push a fact back at somebody who denies it: the shops "did give" four hundred meals a week. "gave" reports the same fact but insists on nothing, so it does not answer the claim. "did gave" keeps the past ending on the main verb although did has already taken the tense; after did the verb returns to its base form. "were giving" turns the fact into an action in progress and, being a continuous, cannot carry the emphatic did at all.

questions.prompt: Which word names the act of providing a permanent fund whose income pays for something year after year?
questions.explanation: An endowment is the act of providing a permanent fund, and what pays year after year is the income of that fund, never the fund itself: that is exactly what makes it permanent. "a donation" is one single act of presenting something as a gift, and nothing stays behind to earn anything. "fund-raising" is the work of soliciting contributions from other people, so it names the collecting and not the fund it feeds. "solidarity" names the fellowship that comes from shared responsibilities and interests, which is a feeling rather than an act of giving.
